name: Carla Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the crusher feed at the large mine, keeping the belt supplied without letting big rock jam the chute. I have a vocational certificate and years on this equipment, though the rate here sits low for someone experienced. My partner Emil drives a school bus, and our children are grown and away. A new boiler used up most of our savings, so we have less than a month's expenses left. Few mines nearby need another crusher operator; I have never used an AI tool, and when something sounds wrong I slow the belt and call maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little computer help with forms is fine as long as the crusher crew still decides when to stop the belt. I don't want every routine improvement sold to us as a miracle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mild AI change probably leaves my shift alone, but our money is already tight after the boiler. Emil's bus pay is steady during term and thinner in school breaks, and one more house bill would put us behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the crusher feed and marking every jam in the paper log. This month Emil and I would list the bills by due date, and in the first year I'd ask payroll to explain why my experienced rate trails the local scale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel tense about the bank balance, not the small AI change. The sound of the belt settling after a jam is easier to deal with than an unexpected bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask payroll?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring my certificate and years of service, then ask what step on the pay scale I actually hold. A clear answer might show whether I should ask the manager for a correction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your children help with bills?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children are grown and managing their own homes. I wouldn't turn a boiler into their problem unless we truly ran out of choices.

say: I would keep **stop decisions** with the crusher crew.
I would question big claims about minor **form changes**.
think: My shift looks safe, but the **boiler bill** emptied our cushion.
Emil’s school-break **pay** leaves household income uneven.
do: Keep feeding the **crusher** on each shift and logging every jam in the paper record.
List household bill dates with Emil and ask payroll about the **experienced operator rate**.
feel: I feel **tense** about money, though AI adds little here.
S0.quote: The sound of the belt settling after a jam is easier to deal with than an unexpected bill.
fieldNote: Her **thin cushion** follows a boiler replacement, while term-time bus pay adds ordinary uncertainty.
She values clear **pay information** and direct equipment judgment over claims about small software gains.

steps.text: Keep operating the crusher feed and recording jams
Ask payroll to explain her experienced-operator pay rate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that office software can order parts faster, but it must not turn a six-person shift into five without checking breakdown cover. If the new schedule looks sound, I will use it; I just want someone to show me the evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buying and planning are exactly where the mine can save staff time. I worry the manager may take a crusher shift off the board, and there are few other mines close enough for Emil to keep his bus route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor for the shift plan and compare it with the last three jam reports. If my hours fell in the first year, Emil and I would stop paying for the sports package, and I'd ask the cement works whether its crusher has a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, mostly because I cannot absorb a month without full pay. I don't enjoy learning new screens, but I could follow one if an experienced colleague walked me through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would walk you through the screen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Marta from maintenance because she knows the old log and the new display. I am slow with software, and I would rather admit that than press the wrong stop button.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for another mine job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a rumour. A move would end Emil's bus route and take a deposit we don't have, so the cement works is the realistic first call.

say: I would ask for evidence before changing **crusher staffing**.
I would accept a tested **schedule** after a colleague explains it.
think: My own **hours** could shrink as office planning improves.
Few nearby mines make a lost shift hard to **replace**.
do: Compare the **shift plan** with recent jam reports.
Cancel sports television if hours fall and ask the **cement works** about vacancies.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a month without full pay.
S1.quote: I am slow with software, and I would rather admit that than press the wrong stop button.
fieldNote: She would accept a **proven screen** but wants a trusted maintenance colleague to teach her.
The **cement works** is a concrete nearby option; moving would disrupt Emil’s income and require a deposit.

steps.text: Compare the proposed crusher roster with three recent jam reports
Cancel the sports package if crusher hours fall
Ask the cement works about an available crusher job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the supervisor that thinking AI by 2028 might change buying and schedules, while capable crusher robots come about 2031. I would ask for the equipment dates and which operators the mine plans to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the new crusher controls to take most of the ordinary feed jobs by 2031. At 60 and then 63 I would still need wages; with less than a month saved and few local openings, I lie awake wondering which bill we could pay if my shift disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the manager this week for a written crusher plan and take our household bills to a public employment adviser. If shifts fell in 2028, I'd apply at the cement works and keep every safe paid mine shift in 2029; I would enroll in funded plant-maintenance training if an actual local vacancy were tied to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed and angry at how little time the first date gives us. I know the feed line, but the family budget cannot wait for a promise to turn into a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Emil hear tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Emil that we need a list of what the mine knows, not a guess from the break room. His bus income covers part of the month, but not the mortgage on its own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marta showed me how a blocked chute is cleared safely. If the cement works or mine paid to teach that work and posted a job, I would try it; I wouldn't buy a course on faith.

say: I would demand **equipment dates** and clear staffing plans.
I would explain that **2028 schedules** change before crusher robots around 2031.
think: I expect ordinary **feed jobs** to disappear around 2031.
Our tiny cushion and few local jobs put the **mortgage** at risk.
do: Request a written **crusher plan** and consult a public employment adviser.
Apply at the cement works and take **funded maintenance training** if tied to a vacancy.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and lose sleep over which bills we could pay.
S2.quote: I know the feed line, but the family budget cannot wait for a promise to turn into a job.
fieldNote: She anticipates a major **wage loss** by the robot date and describes lost sleep over bills.
**Maintenance training** requires funding and a local vacancy; a course alone does not guarantee work.

steps.text: Ask the mine manager for a written crusher replacement plan
Meet a public employment adviser about paid local work
Apply for crusher work at the cement works if shifts fall
Enroll in funded plant-maintenance training if linked to a posted local job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2031 for thinking AI and about 2034 for crusher robots give the mine time to set out fair rules. I would ask for a proper trial on the feed line before management calls the machine safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when the office changes and 66 when the crusher can run itself. Retirement sounds close, but our savings do not cover even a month today, and I cannot assume a pension figure I have never checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my current shift and ask payroll for my retirement estimate in writing. If a proven control system arrived, I'd ask Marta to show me its stop procedure; in 2032 I'd apply for a plant role at the cement works, and after robots arrived I'd keep paid maintenance-assistant work if a real post opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried, but five years gives me time to learn the stop controls properly. The question is whether the mine will pay people during that learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in a trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would stand with Marta at the panel and mark every jam and stop time. If it handles the same bad rock safely for months, I would accept the result.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after Emil and I compare actual income with the mortgage and bills. I cannot let a machine purchase decide a retirement we cannot afford.

say: I would ask for a measured **feed-line trial** before a safety claim.
I would put physical crusher automation around **2034**.
think: Retirement at **66** is uncertain with less than one month saved.
I need a written **income estimate** before leaving paid work.
do: Request a **retirement estimate** and continue the crusher shift.
Learn proven stop controls with Marta and apply at the **cement works**.
feel: I feel **worried**, while five years offers time to learn safely.
S3.quote: I cannot let a machine purchase decide a retirement we cannot afford.
fieldNote: She separates a **robot date** from a financially possible retirement date.
Her willingness to learn **controls** depends on a sustained safety trial and help from maintenance.

steps.text: Request a written retirement-income estimate from payroll
Learn a proven crusher stop procedure with maintenance colleague Marta
Apply for a plant role at the cement works in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that thinking AI in 2036 and crusher robots around 2039 leave a decade to sort out staffing and retirement. The mine should put its dates in writing while people still have years to make choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when the office changes and 71 when robots run the feed. I might have stopped by then, but the boiler bill showed me how quickly savings go, so I will not call retirement certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep operating the crusher while my hearing and reactions are safe, and Emil and I would review our bills each year. In 2037 I'd compare the retirement estimate with the mortgage before reducing shifts; if it fell short, I'd ask the cement works for paid work rather than stop earning because a calendar says 68.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed by the robot itself. The low rate and our nearly empty savings still make the present feel tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you save more now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put aside a little from any extra shifts after the boiler instalment ends. At the moment that instalment has to be paid first, so I won't promise a number I cannot keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is your limit for working longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my hearing misses a warning horn, I stop operating. I would ask for a safer paid task, but I won't trade someone else's safety for one more wage packet.

say: I would request written **mine equipment dates** while older workers still have years to plan.
I would place crusher robots around **2039**, three years after the thinking change.
think: I may have retired by **71**, but savings do not prove it.
The low rate and near-empty **cushion** still press on us now.
do: Continue safe **crusher work** and review household bills annually.
Compare income with the **mortgage** in 2037 before reducing shifts.
feel: I feel **less rushed** by robots, though money remains tight.
S4.quote: I will not call retirement certain.
fieldNote: The distant robot date does not erase her **present money pressure** or hearing-safety limit.
Any extra **saving** depends on an instalment ending and additional shifts, which she does not assume.

steps.text: Keep operating the crusher while hearing and reactions remain safe
Compare written retirement income with the mortgage in 2037
Set aside extra-shift pay after the boiler instalment ends

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the mine could decide on staffing before we have any cushion to use. Written equipment dates, a local paid training route and an honest wage estimate would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens if the warning horn is drowned out by the belt. I would stop the crusher line before I let a worker walk into a moving chute.

headlineQuote: I would stop the crusher line before I let a worker walk into a moving chute.
portrait: Carla is an **experienced crusher operator** at a large mine, paid below the usual rate.
She and Emil have grown children but less than **one month** of expenses saved after a boiler replacement.
She has never used **AI tools** and wants trusted help before using new controls.
She checks **written plans**, local cement-works work and real retirement income before leaving her shift.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because staffing could change before she rebuilds a cushion.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **written dates**, local paid training and a reliable income estimate.
